client: I’ve been feeling really anxious about my final exams next month. I haven’t been able to stick to my study schedule, and now I’m worried I’m going to fail. Honestly, I’m not sure if talking about it will help—I feel like I just need to study more, but I can’t seem to focus.
therapist:
I hear the urgency and distress in your voice as you talk about these exams—it sounds like you're really putting pressure on yourself. Let's pause for a moment and examine whether these thoughts about failing are based on facts or fears.  

You mentioned struggling to focus—what do you think might be making it harder to concentrate right now?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, fast speech

client: I think the fear of failing is mostly in my head, but it feels so real when I’m sitting down to study. I keep imagining the worst-case scenarios, like completely blanking during the exam or not finishing on time. As for focusing, I think it’s because I’m so overwhelmed—there’s so much material, and I don’t even know where to start. It’s like my brain just shuts down.
therapist:
The rapid pace and higher pitch in your voice tell me how overwhelming this feels—it's like your thoughts are racing as fast as your words.  

It makes sense that your brain "shuts down" when flooded with worst-case scenarios and endless material. Could we try breaking this into smaller pieces together? What’s one topic that feels manageable to tackle first?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: I guess statistics would be the easiest to start with since I at least understand the basics. But even that feels like too much—what if I spend time on it and still don’t do well? Part of me thinks I should jump to the hardest topics first, but then I just panic and procrastinate. This is why I never stick to plans.
therapist:
Your voice sounds both tentative and rushed, like you're torn between wanting to make progress and fearing it won’t be enough.  

It’s understandable to feel stuck between starting with what’s easier or diving into the hardest parts—that kind of pressure can make anyone procrastinate. Let’s focus on statistics for now and see if breaking it into smaller steps helps ease the panic. What’s one small thing you could do today to get started?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I could start by reviewing the first chapter of my statistics textbook. But even that feels like it won’t be enough—what if I end up spending hours on it and still don’t remember anything? I feel like I’m wasting time if I’m not studying everything at once. It’s hard to shake the idea that I need to do it all perfectly.
therapist:
Your voice sounds both rushed and a little deflated, like you’re trying to push through but also doubting yourself every step of the way.  

It’s tough when perfectionism tells you that anything less than doing everything at once isn’t good enough. What if we reframe this as progress, not perfection? Even reviewing one chapter is a step forward—what’s one thing you could remind yourself to ease that pressure?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I guess I could remind myself that doing something is better than doing nothing. But it’s hard to believe that when it feels like the stakes are so high. Part of me worries that if I don’t study everything perfectly, I’ll regret it later. It’s like I’m setting myself up for failure no matter what I do.
therapist:
Your voice sounds tense and hurried, like you’re caught in a cycle of doubt and pressure.  

It’s understandable to feel this way when the stakes feel so high, but perfectionism often traps us in all-or-nothing thinking. What if we focus on progress, not regret? Even small steps forward can build momentum—what’s one thing that could help you trust that doing something is enough for today?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Maybe I could remind myself that even reviewing one chapter will help me feel more prepared than I do right now. But it’s hard to trust that because I’ve always felt like I need to do everything perfectly to succeed. What if I still don’t do well, even after putting in the effort? That’s what scares me the most.
therapist:
Your voice sounds both thoughtful and a little shaky, like you’re trying to hold onto hope but still feel the weight of uncertainty.  

It’s brave to acknowledge that fear of not doing well even after your effort—that’s a tough feeling to sit with. What if we explore what "success" looks like for you beyond perfection? Could it include things like feeling more prepared or simply knowing you tried your best?

client: I guess success could mean feeling more confident going into the exam, even if I don’t get a perfect grade. But it’s hard to let go of that idea of perfection—I’ve always tied my self-worth to doing well academically. It feels like if I don’t excel, I’m not good enough.
therapist:
Your voice sounds both determined and a little shaky, like you’re wrestling with this idea of perfection while also trying to hold onto a new perspective.  

It’s powerful that you’re considering success as feeling more confident, even without perfection—that’s a big shift. Let’s explore what “good enough” could look like for you, beyond grades. What might it feel like to untangle your self-worth from academic performance?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, fast speech

client: It’s hard to imagine what “good enough” looks like outside of grades because I’ve always used them as a measure of my worth. Maybe it could mean being kinder to myself or recognizing that I’m trying my best, even if it’s not perfect. But honestly, that feels so abstract—I’m not sure how to actually believe it.
therapist:
Your voice sounds thoughtful but a little uncertain, like you’re trying to grasp this idea but it still feels out of reach.  

It’s a big step to even consider being kinder to yourself—that’s not easy when you’re used to measuring your worth by grades. What if we start small: what’s one thing you could say or do today to remind yourself that trying your best is enough, even if it feels abstract right now?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I could try writing down something like, “Trying my best is enough,” and putting it where I’ll see it while I study. It’s okay to feel like you’re going through the motions at first—shifting a mindset takes time, and writing that reminder is a great first step. What if we focus on noticing how it feels to see those words, even if belief doesn’t come right away? Every small step counts.
